4.2  Temporal Difference Learning We train the acquisition network f θ f_{\theta} using real and LBO transitions
(Appendix A.7 ).
Each transition provides an observed discovery count and a successor
state, supplying a learning signal for the acquisition function to adapt
its selection strategy to different response landscapes. Real transitions. After querying batch A t A_{t} , we obtain observations O t O_{t} and
discovery count R t R_{t} . We refit the surrogate on D t + 1 D_{t+1} and construct the
successor selection state s t + 1 s_{t+1} . With successor
value weight w t w_{t} , the round is stored as the training record ξ t = ( s t , A t , R t , w t , s t + 1 ) . \xi_{t}=(s_{t},A_{t},R_{t},w_{t},s_{t+1}). Virtual transitions through LBO. Screening follows a single trajectory, which cannot be reset to
test alternative selection sequences within the same budget.
Each round therefore provides only one real batch transition.
LBO supplements these transitions by temporarily hiding measured
outcomes and then restoring them to reconstruct experimental
feedback. Let D + D^{+} and U + U^{+} denote the current measured dataset and
unmeasured pool. For a batch A A of measured candidates, hiding its
outcomes gives D − = D + ∖ { ( x , e ⁡ ( x ) ) : x ∈ A } . D^{-}=D^{+}\setminus\{(x,e(x)):x\in A\}. We refit the surrogate model on D − D^{-} to construct the predecessor state s − s^{-} ,
and construct the successor state s + s^{+} from D + D^{+} with the outcomes restored.
The discovery count R R is computed from the batch’s observed outcomes.
We compute w w by comparing hit probability estimates before and after
restoration over U + U^{+} .
The resulting virtual transition is ξ ~ = ( s − , A , R , w , s + ) \widetilde{\xi}=(s^{-},A,R,w,s^{+}) .
Real and virtual transitions enter the same replay buffer ℛ \mathcal{R} ,
providing more training data without additional experiments. Feedback weights. For each candidate, hit and nonhit probabilities define a
Bernoulli distribution. For both real and virtual transitions, we use
Hellinger distance ( Hellinger, 1909 ) to compare these
distributions before and after feedback over the remaining pool.
Unchanged predictions across U t + 1 U_{t+1} give w t = 0 w_{t}=0 , while larger Hellinger distances assign
more weight to successor value: w t 2 = ∑ x ∈ U t + 1 H Ber 2 ​ ( p ^ t ​ ( x ) , p ^ t + 1 ​ ( x ) ) | U t + 1 | , H Ber 2 ​ ( p , q ) = 1 − p ​ q − ( 1 − p ) ​ ( 1 − q ) . w_{t}^{2}=\frac{\sum\nolimits_{x\in U_{t+1}}H_{\mathrm{Ber}}^{2}(\hat{p}_{t}(x),\hat{p}_{t+1}(x))}{|U_{t+1}|},\qquad H_{\mathrm{Ber}}^{2}(p,q)=1-\sqrt{pq}-\sqrt{(1-p)(1-q)}. sections.heading: C.1  Datasets and Hit Definitions
sections.text:
C.1  Datasets and Hit Definitions The eight public screens comprise four single gene tasks, three double gene
tasks, and one triple gene task, covering T cell function, cancer
cell growth, immune killing, and genetic interactions. Each candidate is
a single gene or combinatorial perturbation. Table C1 summarizes perturbation types, phenotypes, and hit rules. Table C1: Perturbation types, phenotypes, and hit rules for eight tasks. Dataset Perturbation Phenotype Hit rule IFN- γ \gamma ( Schmidt et al., 2022 ) Single gene IFN- γ \gamma production by T cells Top 5% by absolute score IL-2 ( Schmidt et al., 2022 ) Single gene IL-2 production by T cells Top 5% by absolute score NK ( Zhuang et al., 2019 ) Single gene Cancer cell sensitivity to NK cell killing Top 5% by absolute score Carnevale ( Carnevale et al., 2022 ) Single gene T cell proliferation under adenosine suppression Top 5% by absolute score Simpson K562 ( Simpson et al., 2023 ) Two genes K562 cell growth after dual gene repression Top 5% by raw score SCHEMATIC ( Fong et al., 2025 ) Two genes Genetic interactions across cancer cell backgrounds Bottom 5% by raw score Kuzmin yeast ( Kuzmin et al., 2020 ) Three genes Genetic interactions in triple gene yeast perturbations Bottom 5% by raw score Horlbeck Jurkat ( Horlbeck et al., 2018 ) Two genes Jurkat cell growth after dual gene repression Bottom 5% by raw score Raw phenotype scores are transformed into effects e ⁡ ( x ) e(x) according to the
direction in the table. For a pool of N = | 𝒳 | N=|\mathcal{X}| candidates, the score
at rank max ⁡ { 1 , ⌊ 0.05 ​ N ⌋ } \max\{1,\lfloor 0.05N\rfloor\} in descending effect order defines
the fixed threshold τ \tau , with hits given by z ( x ) = 𝟏 { e ( x ) ≥ τ } z(x)=\mathbf{1}\{e(x)\geq\tau\} . The target hit proportion is 5%, and τ \tau is the corresponding phenotype score threshold. The threshold is
fixed before screening. The phenotype and hit label of each candidate are
revealed when it is queried. IFN- γ \gamma . This task identifies genes that regulate interferon- γ \gamma production in
T cells. Enrichment differences between populations with high and low cytokine levels
measure perturbation effects. We target strong effects in either direction ( Schmidt et al., 2022 ) . IL-2. This task identifies regulators of interleukin-2 production following T cell
stimulation. Enrichment differences between populations with high and low expression define the phenotype, with strong effects in either direction
included as discovery targets ( Schmidt et al., 2022 ) . NK. This task studies cancer cell genes that affect sensitivity or resistance
to natural killer cells. The phenotype is the sum of standardized enrichment
scores across two replicates for perturbed K562 cells exposed to NK cells
relative to controls. Strong effects in either direction are targeted ( Zhuang et al., 2019 ) . Carnevale. This task studies genes that affect T cell proliferation under
immunosuppressive conditions. We use enrichment scores associated with proliferation
from the screen under adenosine suppression and target perturbations that
strongly increase or decrease proliferation ( Carnevale et al., 2022 ) . Simpson K562. The original study examines how DNA repair genes jointly affect cell growth
and PARP inhibitor response. We use its double gene CRISPRi growth phenotype
and target combinations with the highest growth scores ( Simpson et al., 2023 ) . SCHEMATIC. This task seeks gene combinations that cause synthetic lethality across cancer cell
backgrounds. We use the multilineage interaction score to identify strong
negative interactions whose growth or survival defects exceed expectations
from individual perturbations ( Fong et al., 2025 ) . Kuzmin yeast. This task examines how duplicate genes compensate for one another and how
this compensation depends on other genes. We use the corrected trigenic
interaction score to target combinations with stronger growth defects than
expected ( Kuzmin et al., 2020 ) . Horlbeck Jurkat. This task examines the effect of jointly repressing two genes on Jurkat
cell growth. We use the double gene CRISPRi growth phenotype and target
combinations that strongly inhibit growth ( Horlbeck et al., 2018 ) .
